what_its_for: Siponimod is used to treat adults with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (SPMS), a form of MS that gets worse over time. It helps slow down the worsening of disability and reduces the number of MS flare-ups (relapses) you experience. It works by keeping certain immune cells inside your lymph nodes so they cannot travel to your brain and spinal cord and cause damage.
how_to_take: Take siponimod by mouth once daily, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. When you first start this medicine, your doctor will have you take a starter pack with lower doses for the first 5 days. This is called the titration period and it helps your heart adjust to the medicine safely. Do NOT skip the starter pack or jump straight to your regular dose.
dosing: The usual maintenance dose is 2 mg once daily. However, before you start, your doctor will do a genetic test (CYP2C9 genotype test) to find out how your body processes this medicine. Some patients are prescribed 1 mg once daily instead, based on their genetic results. During the first 5 days (titration period), you will take smaller doses that gradually increase: Day 1 and Day 2: 0.25 mg, Day 3: 0.5 mg, Day 4: 0.75 mg, Day 5: 1.25 mg, Day 6 onward: your regular maintenance dose. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose during the first 6 days of treatment, call your doctor right away. You may need to restart the starter pack from the beginning to protect your heart. If you miss a dose after your first 6 days of treatment, just skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time the following day. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose. If you stop taking siponimod for 4 or more days in a row, call your doctor before restarting — you may need to begin the starter pack again.
storage: Store siponimod tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original packaging. Protect them from moisture and heat. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not store in the bathroom. Dispose of unused or expired tablets safely — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid live vaccines while taking siponimod and for at least 4 weeks after stopping it, as this medicine weakens your immune system and live vaccines could cause serious infections. Talk to your doctor about getting all recommended vaccines at least 1 month before starting this medicine. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially those with chickenpox or shingles, as your immune system may not fight infections as well as usual. Avoid getting pregnant while taking this medicine — siponimod can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 10 days after your last dose. Tell your doctor if you plan to become pregnant. Avoid starting this medicine if you have had a recent heart attack, stroke, or certain heart rhythm problems, or if you are taking certain other medicines — your doctor will review all your medications first.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: a slow or irregular heartbeat or feel dizzy, lightheaded, or faint (especially in the first few days); sudden vision changes or blurry vision (a rare but serious eye problem called macular edema can occur); signs of infection such as fever, chills, body aches, or sores that won't heal; signs of meningitis such as severe headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light, nausea, or confusion; shortness of breath or swelling in your legs; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain; new or worsening neurological symptoms after stopping this medicine; or any new or unusual symptoms that concern you. If you are pregnant or become pregnant while taking this medicine, call your doctor immediately.
when_it_works: Siponimod starts working in your body fairly quickly, but you may not notice visible changes right away. The medicine begins to reduce immune activity within hours of taking it. However, its effects on slowing disability progression and reducing relapses are measured over months and years. Most people do not feel a dramatic change suddenly — the benefit is seen over time through fewer relapses and slower worsening of MS. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you do not notice immediate changes.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do NOT use siponimod if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 10 days after stopping. Breastfeeding: It is not known if siponimod passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Older Adults (65+): Use with caution. Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially heart-related effects. Kidney or Liver Problems: Patients with severe liver problems should not take this medicine. Patients with mild to moderate kidney or liver issues may still be able to take it — your doctor will decide. Heart Conditions: This medicine can slow your heart rate, especially when you start taking it. Patients with certain pre-existing heart conditions may not be able to take siponimod safely. Your doctor will monitor your heart (with an ECG) when you begin treatment. Genetic Testing: A blood test must be done before starting this medicine to determine your CYP2C9 gene type, as this affects your dose. Patients with a certain gene variant (CYP2C9*3/*3) should NOT take siponimod.
